subject: Practical lack of ergodicity vs slow convergence

messages.subject: Practical lack of ergodicity vs slow convergence
parts:
Hi,

I have a query related to ergodicity of Markov Chains over a continuous support. Suppose we were considering using Metropolis sampling (sorry this example is easier said considering this, rather than HMC), and you had two areas of high probability mass, separated by a large area of very low, yet still finite mass. 

If I were to specify a very small width for the proposal/jumping distribution, then it will take a very long time for the sampler to explore the typical set; resulting in slow convergence to the true distribution. My question is this: would one say that the Markov Chain is (practically) non-ergodic here, since it would essentially take an infinity of time to converge?

If not, can you advise me on a continuous example that is truly non-ergodic? Thinking of discrete examples is easy, but am having a harder time thinking of continuous ones.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Practical lack of ergodicity vs slow convergence
parts:
tl;dr: Markov chains will almost always be ergodic.  What we care
about in practice isn’t ergodicity but rather the type of ergodicity.

Firstly, what you describe is not “Metropolis sampling”.  The Metropolis
algorithm, and its generalization Metropolis-Hastings, is a general 
algorithm for constructing a Markov chain.  Indeed Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo can be considered a Metropolis algorithm.  To what you refer is
_Random Walk Metropolis_.

Now on to your question.  Ergodicity is simply the guarantee that the
Markov chain will coverage to the target distribution asymptotically.
More specifically, for any given subset of the target parameter space
and initial point there exists some finite number of iterations where
the Markov chain initialized as the initial point has explored that
entire subset.  Of course that number of iterations could be insanely
large and impractical, but still finite, so at no point are we talking about 
infinite times.

There are various way to obstruct even this ergodicity, the two easiest
being reducibility and periodicity.  If the Markov chain is reducible then
the target parameter space can be partitioned into subsets, and the
Markov cannot escape the partition in which is starts.  A periodic chain
will get stuck in a loop that explores only a small number of states.

Luckily these conditions are easily remedied by adding small tweaks
to a Markov transition.  Ultimately it’s really, really hard for a Markov
chain to not be ergodic if the target distribution is well-behaved.

But ergodicity alone may not be sufficient in practice, as we only have
computational resources for a finite number of iterations.  What we really
want to ensure good finite-iteraiton behavior are strong ergodicity results, 
such as geometric ergodicity, which ensure that the Markov chain converges
to the target distribution at a geometric rate.  Proving that a Markov chain and
a target distribution are geometrically ergodic is really, really, really hard.
Usually we instead try to identify features that obstruct geometric ergodicity
(such as heavy tails) and try to diagnose those features in practice.  Some
colleagues and I are actively working on this for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

Now, all of that said, even geometric ergodicity can be insufficient in practice.
For example, consider a multimodal distribution as you suggested.  All
geometric ergodicity says is that you can find the modes really quickly, but
it doesn’t guarantee that you can sample between the modes all that well
(i.e. the Markov chain converges at a geometric rate, but that rate is really,
really slow).  

Ultimately, Markov chains are subtle objects and that subtlety matters a
lot more in practice than most people consider.  We’re trying to identify
what matters and turn the into automatic diagnostics to improve the 
robustness of these algorithms, but it’s an ongoing process.
